## Lab 7

In this lab we will practice working with raster data, in this case in the context of climate models. I have given you 4 sets of data:

1. Climate Model Data_Historic - this is a NetCDF file with output from a climate model. Data is monthly average air temperature for 1920-2005

2. Climate Model Data_Future - this is a NetCDF file with climate model output for the period 2006-2080

3. Observed Temp Data - this is gridded data based on weather station and satellite data. Data is monthly for 1991-2000

4. Population data - gridded counts of population for a number of years

The first part of the lab will compare modeled and observed climate data for major cities around the world. The second part of the lab will combine the population data and future climate data to project future changes in global temperature.


3b. Note that this climate model data is for 1920-2005 but the observation data is only from 1991-2000. Subset the climate model data to just the years 1991-2000. Also change the units to match those of the observed climate data.

```{r}
# hint: have a look at ?terra::time to see how to get years

# time(R_Data_Historic) gives values back.  year,month,day format given
time_values <- time(R_Data_Historic) #place time values in vector

#keep values from 1991-2000. Note this part is purely the boolean vector/logical vector (True/False)
time_boolean<- time_values >= as.Date("1991-01-01") & time_values <= as.Date("2000-12-31")

# subset layers, for every True value, keep the layer
time_2000 <- R_Data_Historic[[time_boolean]]

```

5b. Use `tidyr::pivot_longer` to turn both data-frames into tidy data-frames, with one row for each unique city-month combination

```{r}
#Hint: you want to use the first 10 columns (cities) to pivot (cols argument in the pivot_longer function). Use the values_to argument to name the temperature data column either "observed" or "simulated".

#turn dfs into tidy dfs. tidyverse already loaded 

##frame: city_obs <- ________

city_obs_long <- city_obs %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = 1:10, #alternatively, can't I do -time? > ask Prof RH
               names_to = "city",
               values_to = "observed")

##frame: city_sim <- ________

city_sim_long <- city_sim %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = 1:10,
               names_to = "city",
               values_to = "simulated")
```

5c. Notice that the modeled and observed rasters have used slightly different conventions for naming the months. You can see this in the "name" column of the two data frames you made in 5b. The model output uses the first of the month (e.g. 1991.02.01) whereas the observational data uses the middle of the month (e.g. 1991.01.16). This is a problem since we want to merge together the two data frames to compare observed and simulated data.

To merge the two data frames together, first we need to "chop off" the last two digits in the month ids in both data frames. One way to do this is to use the `substr` function to return some subset of a character vector.

change the variable "time" from Date to "yearmon" (character)

```{r}

#keep only year and month. note that its going to be in xxxx-xx-xx format, where year-month-day
city_obs_long <- city_obs_long %>%
  mutate(yearmon = substr(as.character(time), 1, 7)) #7 is where year and month end, chopping odd last two digits 

city_sim_long <- city_sim_long %>%
  mutate(yearmon = substr(as.character(time), 1, 7))

#check results
head(city_obs_long$yearmon)
head(city_sim_long$yearmon)

```

5d. Merge the observed and modeled city data into a single data-frame. In this case you could use `cbind`, but that it is safer to use `merge`

```{r}
#Hint: you will want to specify two columns in the "by" argument in merge(). Think about what two columns those should be (i.e. what combination of columns identifies a unique observation that matches across the two dataframes)
#rename  df_merged as all_city

all_city <- merge(city_obs_long, #observed city data
                   city_sim_long, #modeled city data
                   by = c("city", "yearmon")) 

```

5e. Make a plot showing observed vs modeled temperature for the 10 cities. Add a 1:1 line which showing the perfect match between observed and modeled data that one would like to see. You can use base plot or ggplot.

```{r}

R_Data_Historic #is in Kelvins

#units do not match. I am going to go ahead and turn K into C in a clean df "all_city_clean"

all_city_clean <- all_city %>%

```


```{r}

ggplot(all_city_clean, 
       aes(x = observed, y = simulated, color = city))+ #define axis' 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)+ #alpha at 0.5 for transparency, since there are many overlapping values
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black")+ #create 1 x 1 line

       x = "Observed Temperature",
       y = "Modeled Temperature",
       color = "City")+ #color by city
  theme_minimal()
```

In the second part of the lab, we will use projections of future temperature change (until 2080) and a map of the distribution of population in 2020 to get global, population-weighted projected warming.

6a. Read in the netCDF file with projected climate model temperature (in the "Climate Model Data_Future" directory) as a SpatRaster. Use the rotate() function again as you did in 1b to transform the coordinates to -180 to 180 and the units to C. Use `subds="TREFHT"`. This has gridded projections of monthly global temperature between 2006 and 2020 under a high-emissions scenario (referred to as RCP8.5).

```{r}
#read in netCDF as SpatRaster 
netCDF <- rast("~/Downloads/ESP_106/ESP 106/esp106_CandyGArellano/Week 7/Data/Climate Model Data_Future/b.e11.BRCP85C5CNBDRD.f09_g16.002.cam.h0.TREFHT.200601-208012.nc", subds = "TREFHT")

#look at the extent
ext(netCDF)

```

```{r}
#rotate
netCDF <- rotate(netCDF, left=TRUE)

#check extent
ext(netCDF) #rotation successful 

netCDF #is in Kelvins 

#convert from Kelvin to Celsius 
netCDR <- netCDF - 273.15 
```



6b. Compute the projected _annual_ trend in global climate. Use `tapp` for this temporal aggregation.

```{r}
#PLAN: I am assuming that I need to get a rate of change to represent "trend". I am going to run a regression for project warming over time
 


?tapp
##by using tapp, i can combine the month layers into a year (annual).. index = c(1,1,1,2,2,2). note temporal> aggregating over time 

head(time(netCDF)) #same time format as prev rasters 
tail(time(netCDF))


```

```{r}
#extract time

##monthly time object
t <- time(netCDF)

##creating year groups
yr <- format(t, "%Y")

#aggregate to annual mean 
annual_mean <- tapp(netCDF, #SpatRaster
                    index = yr, #index can be done 
                    fun = mean, #applying mean to average the times into 1 value/layer
                    na.rm = TRUE #remove na values
                    )
#inspect
annual_mean #years are like "X2005" 

#referenced https://r4ds.hadley.nz/datetimes.html, which shows R date formats 

```

```{r}
#area weights 
lat <- init(annual_mean[[1]], "y") #latitude raster 

w_area <- cos(lat * pi /180 ) 
w_area <-mask(w_area, annual_mean[[1]]) #keep weights where the temperatures are not NA values 

#area-weighted global mean temperature per year (aiming for one value per annual layer)
global_mean_aw <- global(annual_mean, ful = "mean", 
                         weights = w_area, na.rm = TRUE) 
```

```{r}
#year vector 
year_vec <- as.integer(sub("^X", "", names(annual_mean)))

#area-weighted global mean 
global_vec <- global_mean_aw[,1]

#df for regression 
df_global <- data.frame(year = year_vec, temp = global_vec)

# run linear regression
lm_global <- lm(temp ~ year, data = df_global)
summary(lm_global)

# slope to represent temp change per year
coef(lm_global)["year"]
```


Use these data in the questions below.

```{r}
pop
```

7b. We want only the 5th layer in this SpatRaster, which corresponds to population count in 2020. (Note - I know this from some associated files that came with the netCDF file. Take a look at the csv file in the directory to see this documentation). Pull out just the population in 2020.

```{r}
#2020 population
pop_2020 <- pop[[5]]

```


8a. Now we want to eventually match the population data to the projected temperature data. But the problem is that the grid size of the climate model is much larger than the spatial resolution of the population data. How many rows and columns does the climate model data have? And how many rows and columns does the population data have? Use code to show that.

```{r}
#rows
nrow(pop_2020) #720
nrow(netCDF) #192
#720 /192 = > approx 4

#columns
ncol(pop_2020) #1440
ncol(netCDF) #288
#1440 / 288 = 5

```


8b. To fix this problem we can aggregate the population raster up to the resolution of the climate model using the `aggregate` function. The population data you have is the population count (i.e. number of people in each grid cell). What function should we use to aggregate to larger grid cells? What function would we use instead if we had population density data instead of population count?

**Answer: We should use sum() for aggregating to larger grid cells. We can mean() if we had population density, since density already depends on a given spac. e**


8c. Aggregate the population data to a higher level of resolution, as close as possible to the climate model data.

```{r}
#aggregate to a grid. exactly matching on cols (4) and using approximation on rows (5)
pop_ag <- aggregate(pop_2020, fact = c(4, 5), fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)

#results
c(nrow(pop_ag), ncol(pop_ag))


```

8d. If everything has gone according to plan, we would expect that summing up all the cells in the population SpatRaster should give us something close to the current population on the planet. Calculate that sum from your aggregated population data and compare to the total population today.

```{r}
#population sum 
pop_sum <- global(pop_ag, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) [1,1] 
pop_sum

#total
current_pop <- 8298978817  #this was a number google gave me
difference <- pop_sum - current_pop
difference_percent <- 100 * difference / current_pop

#inspect
difference_percent

```


9a. Now we will use the population data to do a weighted averaging of the projected temperature data, to get the monthly temperature experienced by the average person between 2006 and 2080. 

One problem is that even after the aggregation, the grids of the population data still don't quite match. Use `terra::resample` to resample the aggregated population data to the climate model grid. 

```{r}
#asking for yearly weighted means. 

#resample aggregated population to the climate model grid
pop_resampled <- resample(pop_ag, netCDF[[1]], method = "near") 

pop_resampled <- pop_resampled %>%
  mask(netCDF[[1]]) 
```

**Answer:**
it is higher now.

9b. Now we can use the population SpatRaster to do a weighted average of the climate model data. Use the global() function to calculate both the global and and the population-weighted average temperature for each year. 

```{r}
#global unweighted annual mean temp
global_mean <- global(annual_mean, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

#population-weighted annual mean temp 
pop_weighted <- global(annual_mean, fun = "mean",
                       weights = pop_resampled, na.rm = TRUE)

#combine as df
df_both <- data.frame(year = as.integer(sub("^X","", names(annual_mean))),
                      global_temp = global_mean[,1],
                      pop_weighted_temp = pop_weighted[,1])


```


Make a graph showing the projected annual trend in global climate. On the same graph show the temperature trend for the entire world, and weighted by population. 


```{r}
#reshape for ggplot. No need for tidyterra functions since these aren't rasters
df_long <- df_both %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(global_temp, pop_weighted_temp),
               names_to = "series",
               values_to = "temp") %>%
  mutate(series = recode(series,
                         global_temp = "Global mean",
                         pop_weighted_temp = "Population-weighted mean"))
```

```{r}
#plot
ggplot(df_long, aes(x = year, y = temp, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Projected Annual Trend in Global Climate",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Temperature (°C)",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```
